chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Talhah ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about two towns from the people of war, for each of them having a king separately. They fought, then they reconciled. Then one of the two kings betrayed his companion, so he came to the Muslims and made peace with them on the condition that he would carry out a military expedition with them against that city.

So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not befitting for the Muslims to be treacherous, nor to instruct others with treachery, nor to fight alongside those who are treacherous. But they should fight the polytheists wherever they find them, and what the disbelievers pact upon them is not allowed upon them.'

key_terms.أَهْلِ الْحَرْبِ: People of war (non-Muslims with whom Muslims have no treaty)
key_terms.عَاهَدَ: To make a covenant or pact

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on treachery and fighting alongside treacherous allies?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the principle of *istifham* (independence of treaties) in Islamic jurisprudence, ruling that the treachery of a polytheist ally does not invalidate the Muslims' own treaty obligations. This establishes that while Muslims must avoid deceit, they are not bound by the specific terms of treaties made by non-Muslims, allowing them to fight polytheists wherever found. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly view that *ghadr* (treachery) is a characteristic of the disbelievers, whereas Muslims maintain fidelity to their own covenants.
